questions.q: A company installs biometric attendance systems to track employee entry/exit times in real time and sends instant alerts to supervisors when an employee is late. Which type of control is this primarily an example of, and why?
questions.a: This is **Concurrent Control** because measurement and corrective action (alert to supervisor) occur **during** the activity (employee attendance) while it is still ongoing, allowing immediate intervention. A wrong answer of "Feedback Control" reveals the student thinks any measurement is feedback, ignoring that feedback acts *after* the activity is complete (e.g., monthly attendance report). A wrong answer of "Feedforward Control" reveals confusion between preventing problems *before* they start (e.g., hiring punctual people) vs. monitoring *during* execution.

questions.q: "Feedforward Control is just another name for Planning because both happen before the action starts." Evaluate this statement with a concrete example showing why it is incorrect.
questions.a: The statement is **incorrect**. Planning *sets* the standards and course of action (e.g., "We will produce 10,000 units with <2% defect rate"). Feedforward Control *ensures the inputs and conditions are right* so the plan can be executed (e.g., "We calibrate machines and train operators *before* production starts so the 2% defect target is achievable"). Planning is **prescriptive** (what should happen); Feedforward Control is **preventive** (making sure capabilities match the plan). A student who agrees with the statement confuses *setting direction* with *securing readiness* — a critical distinction for board exam questions asking to "distinguish between planning and controlling."

questions.q: A textile factory in Surat faces frequent yarn breakage on looms. The management takes three actions: (A) They switch to a higher-grade yarn supplier. (B) They install sensors that stop the loom instantly when tension exceeds a threshold. (C) They analyse monthly defect reports to identify which loom operators need retraining. Classify each action as Feedforward, Concurrent, or Feedback Control.
questions.a:
(A) **Feedforward Control** — changing supplier *before* production starts to prevent defects.
(B) **Concurrent Control** — sensors act *during* weaving to stop defects in real time.
(C) **Feedback Control** — monthly report analysis happens *after* production to improve future cycles.
A student who misclassifies (B) as Feedback fails to see that the loom stoppage occurs **while the cloth is being woven**, not after the batch is finished. A student who calls (A) Feedback confuses *input quality assurance* with *output inspection*.

questions.q: Compare the **cost of correction** and **timeliness of information** across the three control types. Why might a startup with limited capital prefer Feedforward Control over Feedback Control, even though Feedforward requires more upfront investment?
questions.a:
| Control Type | Timeliness of Info | Cost of Correction |
|--------------|-------------------|-------------------|
| Feedforward  | Before activity (earliest) | Lowest (prevents error) |
| Concurrent   | During activity | Medium (stops error mid-process) |
| Feedback     | After activity (latest) | Highest (rework/scrap/delivery failure) |

A startup prefers Feedforward because **preventing a defective product from reaching a customer** (which could destroy reputation and lose the only client) is far cheaper than **recalling, replacing, or litigating** after feedback reveals the defect. The student who says "Feedback is cheaper because you only check samples" misses that **sampling misses defects** and the cost of *one* escaped defect in a startup can be existential. This tests understanding of **risk-cost trade-off**, a favourite CUET/IPMAT case-study angle.

questions.q: "An organisation that relies only on Feedback Control is like a driver who only looks in the rear-view mirror." Critique this analogy. Is it fully accurate? What does it miss about the *necessity* of Feedback Control?
questions.a:
The analogy is **partially accurate but incomplete**. It correctly captures that Feedback Control is **backward-looking** (rear-view mirror) and cannot prevent the accident that already happened. However, it misses that **Feedback Control is indispensable for**:
1. **Validating standards** — Were the speed limits (standards) realistic for this road (environment)?
2. **Improving future plans** — The rear-view mirror shows *why* you drifted (pothole, distraction), so you adjust steering *next time*.
3. **Strategic learning** — Only Feedback reveals systemic issues (e.g., consistent 5% sales shortfall → flawed market assumption in the plan).
A student who calls Feedback "useless" or "only for punishment" fails to see that **without Feedback, Feedforward and Concurrent controls cannot be calibrated**. This is a classic board exam "Comment" question trap.

questions.q: Design a **three-layer control system** for a new cloud-kitchen startup delivering healthy meals in Mumbai. Specify one Feedforward, one Concurrent, and one Feedback control measure, each addressing a different critical success factor (e.g., food safety, delivery time, customer satisfaction). Justify why each measure fits its control type.
questions.a:
**Feedforward (Food Safety):** Mandatory FSSAI certification and HACCP training for all chefs *before* kitchen operations begin. *Justification:* Ensures capability to meet safety standards *before* any meal is cooked — prevents contamination at source.

**Concurrent (Delivery Time):** GPS-integrated order tracking dashboard showing real-time courier location vs. promised ETA; auto-reassigns orders if delay > 5 min. *Justification:* Monitors and corrects *during* the delivery process while the meal is in transit.

**Feedback (Customer Satisfaction):** Weekly NPS (Net Promoter Score) survey + analysis of repeat-order rate by menu item; used to revise recipes and drop low-rated dishes next month. *Justification:* Measures outcome *after* consumption to improve *future* menu planning.

A poor answer lists generic measures (e.g., "check quality") without tying timing to the specific success factor or justifying the control type. This tests **synthesis** — the highest Bloom level — and mirrors CUET case-study questions.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Feedforward, Concurrent, and Feedback Control are three types of ______ control classified by when control is exercised relative to the activity: Feedforward (before), Concurrent (during), and Feedback (after).
Fill in the blank: Imagine you are the ______ of a new Metro rail project in Bengaluru.
What is Feedforward, Concurrent, and Feedback Control? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Feedforward, Concurrent, and Feedback Control are three types of managerial control classified by when control is exercised relative to the activity: Feedforward (before), Concurrent (during), and Feedback (after).

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must be able to classify any given managerial action (e.g., hiring policy, real-time dashboard, annual audit) into the correct control type and justify the classification by explaining the timing of intervention relative to the activity.
